title: Caring for the Heart of the Human Family
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer's main teaching emphasizes the importance of acknowledging and addressing our collective shortcomings as human beings, just like Nakagawa Soen Roshi did with his prostrations to prisoners. This requires cultivating compassion, love, and wisdom to overcome greed, hate, and confusion, ultimately creating a more harmonious and loving world. By embracing our imperfections and letting go of illusions, we can develop true happiness and understanding, transforming ourselves and the world around us through mindfulness and simplicity.

My voice is fading a little.
So if you can't hear, just wave your hand or something.
I'll pretend I'm on Broadway and project.
It's good to be here for our annual three-day, or whatever it is, sesshin, and great to be back in Bellingham and see everyone.
It always cheers me up and makes me feel good.
I'm so thrilled and really happy with the solidness and the strength of this community.
So thank you all.
There's a story that you probably haven't heard.
It's a little obscure story about Nakagawa Soen Roshi, who was a 20th century Japanese teacher, very eccentric and weird and strange and wonderful.
I met him a few times.
He came to America on a number of occasions, although he mostly lived and taught and practiced in Japan.
The story goes that once upon a time he was invited to give a talk at a prison, and he began his talk by making prostrations to the prisoners, bowing many, many times to the prisoners.
After he made all these prostrations, he burst into tears and said to them, "Please forgive me.
Please forgive me.
If we priests had done our job better, you wouldn't be here.
If we had done our jobs as we are supposed to do, you wouldn't have done the things that you did to bring you here.
So it's our fault, and I feel terrible about it, and I'm here to ask for your forgiveness."
That's the story.
This may sound like an exaggeration to you, or weird or strange.
But if you think about it for a little while, it's less strange than it would appear.
Human beings are like a big family, right?
We're pretty much one big family, all related to each other, living on a small planet.
So we're all members of one tremendously dysfunctional family, as we know.
And like all dysfunctional families, the confusion in the family really belongs to everyone.
It's everybody's fault and everybody participates in it.
Although usually we say, "Well, this one or that one is really the one to blame, because she is so impossible.
Nobody could ever deal with her.
She's the reason why everything is so dysfunctional."
And it may be quite true.
She may be very impossible, but the confusion wouldn't be what it is unless everybody participates in it.
And anyway, if you look at that one impossible person, how do you suppose she got that way to begin with?
Of course, she got that way because very early on she was met with reactions, fairly consistent over time, that took a little bit of impossibleness and made it a big quantity of impossibleness.
In other words, her natural drop of craziness became an ocean of craziness because of all the reactions that she got to it over a whole lifetime.
So instead of her family taking this little drop of craziness and healing it and making it better, it made it worse.

If you follow this line of thinking, it might actually make sense to think that the members of the family who are the calmest, wisest, and most committed to goodness are in a way most responsible for the craziness in the family.

And yes, if they had done their job better, if they were somehow a little wiser, a little prouder, a little calmer, a little more skillful, a little more committed to spending the time it takes to bring healing, possibly they would have been able to bring more peace to the family.
This is, I think, what Nakagawa Soen Roshi meant when he made prostrations to the prisoners and cried.
The human family really is a dysfunctional family.
It's exactly like your dysfunctional family and mine.
Altogether, we're one big mess of a dysfunctional family.
And we can see this every day in our newspapers.
I think we all do understand that most of the criminals are not in jail, right?
And most of the people who are in jail are probably not really what we would call criminals.
Probably the real criminals are people who look like very successful politicians and business people and so on.
As bad as you might think our own government is, most governments in the world are way, way worse than ours, even as it stands at this moment.
Corruption and violence are not unusual.
They're commonplace all over the world.
Corruption and violence, now and forever, have been the norm among people who are in control of things.
How does that happen?
Who knows?
One can look at one's own life and see that you want to have some power.
Why do you want power?
For personal gain, for a sense of importance, or maybe out of fear that if you don't have the power, someone else is going to exercise power over you.
So you want a little bit of power, and once you have a little bit of power, you want to maintain it at all costs.
It actually becomes a little bit addictive, that power.
So you want to maintain it and increase it.
It's not too surprising that power grabbing and corruption have always been common.
There's nothing new in this.
It's been going on as long as this human family has existed.
So you might well say, "Ah, I hate human beings."
But if you hate human beings, I'm sorry, but you're one of them.
And you can't really live actually hating yourself and hating human beings.
Although I think these days there are a lot of people who hate human beings and are deeply wounded by human behavior.
But that's really no way to live.
You have to think, honestly, yes, human beings are pretty terrible.
True.
But also, human beings are pretty great.
Also true.
Also true.
What a big surprise.
Human beings are good, and human beings are bad.
Just like you and me.
Every family is like that, right?
We all love our families.
We all know, oh, what a mess.
And we love our families.
Why?
Because we know there's something really good about our families, even though we also know there's something really bad about our families.
So if there's going to be healing in these families, we have to take the good and make it stronger, right?
So that it becomes way stronger than the bad.
This, folks, is a long-range project.
According to the Buddha, we have some good in us, all of us, and we have some bad in us.
The good, he called awakening, which means compassion.
It means love.
It means caring.
It means a kind of clear-eyed wisdom.
It means energy to bring that wisdom out.
And it means generosity to share it with everyone.
The bad, he called greed, hate, and confusion.
Fear.
Lack of courage.
Lack of energy.
Lack of vision.
I've always been moved by the story of the Buddha that, as a young man, in great shape himself, with no problems, he goes out into the world and he sees people's suffering.
It moves him deeply.
He cares, and he takes the suffering of others personally.
And he vows to give up his privileged life in order to do something about it.
What was the first thing he decided to do about this suffering he saw all around him?
He decided to meditate intensely for a very long period of time.
Most people would think that if you care about suffering, pretty much the last thing you would do is meditate intensively for a long period of time.
What good is that going to do anybody?
No.
If you care about the suffering, you go forth into the world and you do something to help.
But the Buddha's thought was that doing that would not work.
Probably the effort to help when there's not enough wisdom, not enough calmness, not enough genuine compassion, won't work out so well.
So he thought, in order to help, the most important thing is to turn the heart around.
Not just my heart, his heart, and your heart, but the whole heart of the whole human family, so that there's more goodness and more compassion than there is greed and hatred.
As long as you try to help based on greed and hatred and fear, even if your motivation is good, even if you think you're doing good, likely in the end it will not work.
This was the Buddha's thought.
How many times have we seen this ourselves, even in our short lives?
How many times have we seen a leader coming to power, promising to do good, and maybe really meaning that, really wanting to do good?
But then pretty soon, that leader is just as bad as all the other ones.
Sometimes a leader comes to power in tremendous enthusiasm, and a period of euphoria gives way to a period of repression.
We've seen this, right?
I've seen it a number of times in my own life.
Because there's not enough goodness in the family.
There's not enough compassion in the family.
There's not enough wisdom in the family to prevent the greed and the fear from holding sway.
That's why the Buddha thought that this process of healing our family has to begin with intense meditation.
He knew that he had to begin by turning his own heart around.
We call this his awakening.
And what did he awaken to?
He awakened to love, to wisdom, to compassion, and to caring.
And he did become a blessing for others.
He remains a blessing for us today.
So in our practice we imagine ourselves just like the Buddha, doing our practice to turn our hearts around, but not just for ourselves.
We're doing it for our families and the whole human family, so that maybe eventually we won't have to have a dysfunctional human world.
After his awakening, the Buddha went forth to help.
He shared his life and his teaching with others every single day.
As far as I can tell from the Sutras, every single day for 45 years, until his passing.
So the Buddha was an activist.
He was really active.
Always on the road.
Always traveling.
Always speaking.
Always encountering others.
Preaching his message of peace, of fairness, of compassion, of caring, of depth, and of wisdom.
And the Sutras show that he was always open to dialogue with anybody.
Even evil rulers.
Even murderers.
He spoke to, and accepted, and opened his heart to them.
After his initial time of intense meditation he continued his daily practice.
I think he did it for himself, for his disciples, and also as an example for everyone of what it looks like to practice a life of devotion and peace.
The Buddha knew from the very beginning that compassion and love is much more than an emotion.
Emotions are much more than emotions, because underlying every emotion is an understanding, an approach to life.
When that understanding and that approach is weak or inaccurate, the emotion will be destabilizing and it will not lead in the direction of goodness, even if it's a positive emotion.
How much trouble has everybody in this room gotten into over love?
Right?
Nobody can complain about love, but think of all the horrible things you did and said and heard from other people over love.
All the pain that came from it.
That's why the Buddha knew that he had to meditate intensely at the beginning, to find a true and a firm basis for his feeling.
We call this basis wisdom.
Prajnaparamita.
It's the teaching of the Heart Sutra.
So the point of meditation practice is not really to find some calmness and peace; it's to develop this wisdom.
Probably we will find some calmness and peace, because in order to develop wisdom you have to have a mind with some stability, depth and peacefulness.
A very jumpy mind might accomplish a lot and do all kinds of creative things, but it won't really bring a depth of wisdom.
It won't really bring clear seeing.
So peace is important and it's pleasant.
It's nice to be peaceful.
At least I think so.
But peace is not the point.
Anyway, peace only lasts as long as things are nice and quiet.
Maybe we can have a nice, peaceful, pleasant retreat here for a few days.
I hope so.
We can all feel peaceful.
We can all live harmoniously together since we're not talking.
I hope I always enjoy retreats.
To me it's one of the great pleasures to come to retreat.
But then soon the retreat is over and we have to face the stress and strain of the dysfunctional world.
And the peace only lasts, maybe we're lucky if it lasts a half an hour.
So yes, I recommend to everybody a little retreat.
It's really good.
Very, very good.
Very important.
But to have a retreat from the crazy world and then think that that's it is clearly not enough.
Our aspiration is more than this.
We really do aspire to turn the world around, to make the world better, to make it kinder and more fair.
That's why we are determined to develop wisdom just the way the Buddha did.
This wisdom, this prajnaparamita, sees life as it actually is, not the way we wish it to be.
It sees that life comes and goes, comes and goes, comes and goes constantly.
Nothing ever stays as it is.
Every moment appears and it disappears in that same instant.
There is no abiding.
The way we usually think of things, our deepest, most abiding thoughts, are wrong.
And the lives that we lead based on these fundamental thoughts are painful.
When we can see life as it really is, we can find strength.
Courage.
And we can face the inevitable disasters that this world will bring.
We can understand how these disasters occur, and we don't need to have any illusions about that.
But we can let go of our wishing and our clutching, of our fear and of our confusion.
And we can, just like the Buddha, you and I, we can do this.
We can go forth in our lives and we can be a blessing for everyone.
That's what we're trying to do.
We're trying to make ourselves into blessings for others.
So this is the spirit of our retreat.
This is what we're after in our retreat.
As we all know, in Zen practice meditation means more than meditation.
Meditation means practicing all the time.

Certainly when we're sitting and breathing quietly, but also when we're standing up, when we're sitting, when we're walking, when we're going to the toilet, when we're lying down to rest, when we're eating, when we're resting, when we're working, when we're cleaning up.
All day long we make the effort to return again and again and again to exactly where we are, and to commit ourselves to exactly what we're doing in that moment.
This present moment, we understand, includes all of the past.
It's all here.
And the potential of the future is all here, in each and every moment.
When we forget to be awake in this moment, we know we've forgotten, and we remind ourselves by coming back to the body and back to the breathing.
We just start over again, all the time.
Maybe in one day of a retreat like this we start over again fifty, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand times.
Starting all over again.
Hearing this you may think, wow, this must be frustrating.
Or boring.
So repetitive.
And it does sound that way when you say it.
But when you live it, it's not that way.
It's mostly joyful.

It's joyful to practice this way, and our life becomes suddenly light as a feather, because we can stop being so obsessed with ourselves, and our problems, and our world's problems, and begin to notice how bright and lovely the world actually is.
And how beautiful, literally beautiful, is every human being.

So in order to live like this we kind of have to give up the idea that I am so and so, and I have such and such a history, and this and that happened, and I feel this way and I feel that way, and these are my preferences and my skills, and these are my shortcomings, and my desires, and my fears, and this is me.
I think we have to pretty much give up that fiction.

Not that all that isn't there, but we have to hold it very lightly, and recognize that despite the habitual persistence of these things, when you look very, very closely, you recognize you don't really know who you are.
You don't really know what's going on.
Because who you are and what's going on is so much more vast and marvelous than you can even imagine.
And you realize after about the second or third day of the retreat, there's no such thing as a retreat.
We're not doing anything.
And we're here to find wisdom, to overcome our own suffering and the suffering of the world.
So I hope in this short retreat that we will all take ourselves more seriously than we usually do.
Now, I'm not advocating that we all go around looking grim and severe and totally lose our sense of humor.
And I'm not saying you shouldn't enjoy the retreat.
In fact, I'm recommending, please enjoy the retreat.
You should enjoy this retreat.
It's a blessing.
But that's not in any way counter to the seriousness that we have to have.

Let us not imagine, in the midst of all of our complicated Zen forms, that we are children again, and that your parents are making the rules, and you are going to break the rules to assert your independence, or follow the rules perfectly to illustrate that you are a very good girl.
No, we're not children.
And despite all appearances, there are no rules.
But there is a way to practice seriously, without self-indulgence.
And I hope we will all take this unusual opportunity to do just that.
The practice that we do in our sesshins is really quite simple.
It is not like all the things that we have learned in our education and our training so far.
Where you learn one step and then the next step, and you accumulate expertise and knowledge and you master the material, the practice that we're doing just isn't like that.
It is radically simple.
It's just sitting.
Just breathing.
Just paying attention.
Just being present.
In a way, you could say there is nothing to it at all.
I was reading a book the other day of Suzuki Roshi talks, and he was talking about meditation forty or fifty years ago.
And it struck me what he was saying.
He said pay attention to the exhale.
He said when you breathe out, just practice letting go.
And then he said practice dying.
So maybe he meant pretend when you exhale that this is your last exhale.
A big peaceful relief.
Nothing else ever to do afterward.
No more living.
No more bother.
Just letting everything go finally, on this exhale.
And then he said it seems we like to inhale more than we like to exhale.
It seems that we like to live more than we like to die.
And he said, and that's our problem.
That's our problem.
We like to live.
But it's impossible just to live.
The only way you can live is to live and die.

When we are willing to live and die, to inhale and exhale, then we can really live, and we can really understand life, and we can have some true happiness, and then we can be of real service to others.
This is wisdom.
This is prajnaparamita.
And it's also meditation.
Jnana paramita, rolled up into one, just as the sixth ancestors said.
Wisdom is meditation.
Meditation is wisdom.
It's not just sitting and breathing.
So, I'm bringing this up because Suzuki Roshi's instruction is really good, don't you think?
I recommend: pay attention to inhaling and exhaling, but especially pay attention to exhaling, and be willing to let go a long, smooth, present, complete exhale all the way to the end.
And after that exhale, should it be your good luck to still be alive, you can rest assured another inhale is going to come, whether you even want it or not, because your life will bring it forth.
And when it comes, now you can really appreciate it.
And now you can know that this inhale is absolutely a gift given just to you, marvelously and for absolutely no reason.
So I want to share with you a short meditation practice.
Maybe we can do this right now.
It's something that I often practice.
Maybe I've told you about it before.
Goodness knows I'm zipping around so much I don't remember what I said to who, when, where, and I've long ago stopped trying to remember.
So maybe I shared this with you before.
It's based on the mindfulness of breathing sutra.
I'm sure many of you have practiced it before.
Our classical Soto Zen practice really is almost nothing.
People think meditation, especially Buddhist meditation, is profound and complicated.
But our practice is not profound and it's not complicated.
It's just being present.
And if you think this over a minute, you would say, well, hold on.
I've always been present anyway, haven't I?
I need to do this?
To be present?
Yeah, you probably have been present anyway all your life.
And yeah, probably the truth is you don't need to do this.
You really don't.
But you have to ask yourself, how's my life doing?
And probably the answer is, eh.
Eh, all right, but not really.
I mean, if we're honest.
We don't tell that to our friends, but if we're honest with ourselves, we have to say, I'm not sure.
My life is so thrilling to me.
So probably it's a good idea to meditate.
But the simplicity of our meditation practice makes it actually quite difficult.
So now I'll give you a more complicated meditation practice, which will be easier.
So here's the way it goes.
It's a practice of being aware of the breath, and it has seven steps.
You don't have to remember the steps.
They follow one after another, so it's easy to remember.
But if you forget, doesn't matter.
And actually, if you only remember one step, you can just practice that one step, and that's enough.
So it begins as we always begin, with being aware of our body sitting here, feeling the body lifting up from within.
Our body wants to be open and uplifted, so we let that happen.
We notice the body, feel any sensations that we would notice, and then establish breathing in the belly.
Inhaling and exhaling.
So here's the first step.
Breathing in, I'm aware I'm breathing in.
And breathing out, I'm aware I'm breathing out.
If you want, you can actually say those words to yourself, but the most important thing is to enact them, and to really be aware.
Especially aware of breathing in and breathing out.
Second step.
Breathing in, I bring peace to my breathing.
And breathing out, I bring peace to my breathing.
And again, you can say those words, but the most important thing is to enact that with every breath.
Third, breathing in, I'm aware of my whole body.
And breathing out, I'm aware of my whole body.
So now you feel the breath illuminating and infused through your whole body, and you feel your body as a whole, illuminated by the breath.
Fourth, breathing in, I bring peace to my body.
And breathing out, I bring peace to my body.
And here, if there's any tension in your body, you can just feel it release and relax.
Fifth, breathing in, I feel joy.
Breathing out, I feel joy.
Joy is an odd word.
I don't think any of us really know what it means.
We usually associate it with intense sensual pleasure.
But I think real joy is something more than this.
So without having any idea about what joy is, just practice like this.
Breathing in, I feel joy.
Breathing out, I feel joy.
And maybe you can discover what joy is.
Sixth, breathing in, I let go.
And breathing out, I let go.
It means if you have been feeling some joy, you let go of the joy.
You let go of everything, just like Suzuki Roshi said, let everything go.
Last breath, and the final step: I am breathing in this moment which is fading.
I am breathing out this moment which is fading.
Breathing in and out in the middle of time.
So that's the practice, and if you want, you can practice it during our retreat.
Seven steps: breathing in, aware of breathing in and out.
Second step, breathing in, bringing peace to breathing.
Third, breathing in, aware of the body.
And fourth, breathing in and out, bringing peace to the body.
Fifth, breathing in and out with joy.
And sixth, breathing in and out with letting go.
And seventh, breathing in and out this fading moment.

So you could actually go through those seven steps, giving each one plenty of time, or stopping at one that seems compelling, just going that far, or just using the one you can remember that seemed important to you.
Anyway, if that helps, you can practice like that.
It's a beautiful practice.
It's something that I go back to all the time.
So I want to end my talk with a little Zen story.
I'm sure you know this story.
In fact, we use this story in our Hossen Shiki ceremonies at home, and I think you use it also here, so you'll hear it on Sunday during the ceremony.
So I thought it'd be appropriate to bring it up.
I'm always tinkering with the translation, so the wording that I'm using here would probably be somewhat different from what is said on Sunday.
You know, the name of our family of Zen groups is called Everyday Zen, and this is the origin of the phrase Everyday Zen, in this story.
Once Matsu asked his teacher Nanquan, what is the way?
Nanquan said, everyday mind is the way.
Matsu must have thought there was more to it than that, so he was a little bit puzzled by that answer.
So he said, if everyday mind is the way, how do I aim for it?
And Nanquan said, if you aim for it, you will be going in the wrong direction.
And Matsu said, how am I supposed to get there?
And Nanquan, with great compassion, said to him, the way is vast and wide.
What does this have to do with grasping thinking?
So Nanquan is teaching us that everyday mind, everyday mind, the mind that you and I experience every single day, is actually vast and wide.

And that our ordinary way of conceiving of our lives as if we were consumers, trying to get full value for every dollar of time we're spending so that we should get something out of it and get a good deal, this kind of grasping thinking that we apply to our own lives and our inner lives doesn't touch what's actually going on every day.
Being a human being is an immense privilege and an immense experience, and almost all of the time we are missing it because we're so absorbed with our ideas and our preferences and our concepts.
To practice everyday Zen is to be present enough for our life that we can really feel this immensity and we can appreciate it.
Even to suffer is a privilege.
To be alive, you have to be alive in order to suffer.
Right?
You have to have a body and a mind and a heart.

So when we practice meditation, when we study sutras, when we chant, when we stay present with our prostrations and all of our Zen activities, when we're practicing together over a long time with teachers and seniors and fellow Sangha members, doing this side by side over a long, long time, this helps us to chase away the cobwebs that always will be in our minds, and it will inspire us to just be ordinary human beings.
Nothing special, nothing important.
Just ordinary human beings.
Vast and wide.
Everyday mind is the way.
All the awakening of all the Buddhas, what could it be other than right here in every moment of time in the middle of our lives, every single day?
If only we could see it.
This is liberation and joy.
And it's no big deal.
It's no big deal.
As soon as it's a big deal, we're consumers again, and we fall out of heaven.
So, my dear friends in the Dharma, you guys inspire me.
You really do.
So let's inspire each other and keep this up.
Not for ourselves.
In fact, that's part of the problem.
If we're practicing to improve ourselves, we're already doomed by that very idea.
Right?
Let's practice for no reason at all, and out of love.
So thank you very much, everybody, for coming.
And good luck in the days ahead.
